newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Cars offer aluminium industry brighter future.
newsitem.headline: Cars offer aluminium industry brighter future.

text.p: Motor industry demand for aluminium could double in the next decade as environmental rules and energy-saving pressures increase, Bernard Legrand, chairman of the European Aluminium Association, said on Wednesday.
This would help offset an expected 2.5 percent fall in European demand for primary aluminium in 1996, surplus world capacity and prices around 2-1/4 year lows.
"The advantages of using aluminium in cars are numerous," Legrand, who is also head of Pechiney's aluminium division, told the association's annual news conference.
Aluminium offers substantial benefits by reducing fuel consumption and emissions through weight savings of up to 50 percent per vehicle, he said.

"Aluminium-intensive vehicles provide lower weight combined with improved safety, improved acceleration, braking performance and handling," Legrand said, adding cars could consume two million tonnes of aluminium by 2005.

At present aluminium is used mainly in luxury or sports cars, such as the Volvo 960 and the Porsche Boxster, but Legrand expected the light metal to be used more widely in standard cars as pressure mounts to reduce emissions.
Nearly all the aluminium used in car frames, radiators, doors and other parts can be recycled without loss of quality and is profitable due to its high scrap value, he added.
But one industry source said that the car industry was hesitant to make major long-term investments in new production lines because of concern about volatile aluminium prices.
Aluminium would be more attractive if hedging mechanisms were developed to provide protection against adverse price swings, the source added.
Legrand said aircraft manufacturers and shipbuilders were also making increasing use of aluminium for economic and environmental reasons.

High-speed aluminium ferries, used on the Irish Sea and between Sweden and Denmark, were providing a new market outlet, he added. The metal was increasingly replacing steel due to its high resistance to salt water corrosion
In the packaging market, Legrand said the use of aluminium drink cans had grown by 14.5 percent annually over the past decade and now accounted for more than half the can market.
Only one in three cans were currently recycled in Europe, compared with two out of three in the United States, but this was expected to rise to more than 50 percent by 2000.
Turning to the overall aluminium industry outlook, Legrand said that Western world production was expected to rise by about five percent in 1996.

But European output was forecast only marginally higher at 3.18 million tonnes with consumption down about 2.5 percent from last year's 5.14 million tonnes. Imports from eastern Europe, mainly Russia, were seen staying at around 2.0 million tonnes.
